prompt: Why does node_modules/ belong in .gitignore instead of being committed?
choices: It is fully regenerable from package.json and the lockfile, and committing it bloats the repo for no benefit
Node.js refuses to run if node_modules is tracked by git
GitHub automatically deletes repos containing a tracked node_modules folder
node_modules contains no files that npm install can recreate

prompt: A teammate accidentally commits and pushes an Android release keystore (.jks) file, then immediately deletes it in a follow-up commit. What is actually true afterward?
choices: The keystore is permanently safe again once the delete commit is pushed
The keystore is still recoverable from the repository's history, so the key must be treated as compromised and rotated
Git automatically strips binary secrets from history on push
Deleting the file reverses the exposure as long as no one has cloned the repo yet today

prompt: After running `git lfs track "*.mp4"` and committing a tracked video file, what does the actual git repository (the packfile/history) store for that file?
choices: The full binary video content, same as a normal git blob
A compressed low-resolution preview of the video
A small text pointer file containing an object ID and size, with the real binary stored in separate LFS storage
Nothing — LFS-tracked files are excluded from git entirely, like .gitignore

prompt: Which of these .gitignore entries is specific to an Xcode/iOS project and would not appear in a typical web project's .gitignore?
choices: node_modules/
DerivedData/
.env
dist/

prompt: A teammate says: "Once git-lfs is installed on my machine, it just automatically handles any large file I add." What's wrong with this claim?
choices: Nothing is wrong, that is exactly how git-lfs works
git-lfs only works on files smaller than 10MB
Which files get LFS treatment is controlled by patterns in .gitattributes (written by `git lfs track`); a file not matched by a tracked pattern is stored as a normal blob regardless of its size
git-lfs must be re-installed before every single commit

prompt: A 200MB video is committed directly to git (no LFS), then deleted in a later commit. Why does the repository stay bloated for every future clone?
choices: It doesn't — deleting a file in a new commit immediately shrinks the repository for everyone
Git keeps the old blob in history/packfiles, so every clone still has to download that 200MB version even though it's not in the current working tree
The video gets automatically converted to an LFS pointer after deletion
git gc removes it automatically on the next commit
